items.title: 7.7 Experiment demonstrating stationary waves using microwaves

source_refs.note: Topic 7.7 with Fig. 7.10 and the microwave-oven box (PDF 156, printed 153). The print says the antinode-to-antinode distance gives the wavelength; the lesson adds that it is half a wavelength.

blocks.text: Microwaves are a form of electromagnetic radiation. They are called micro waves because their wavelengths are typically of the order of millimetres or centimetres, much shorter than radio waves. Stationary waves, also known as standing waves, can be produced by microwaves when they are confined to a specific region or cavity, such as wave guides or resonant chambers; in these structures microwaves bounce back and forth, creating a standing wave pattern with nodes and antinodes. This occurs when the microwave frequency matches the resonant frequency of the cavity.

blocks.text: The stationary waves can be created using microwaves by the following simple method (Fig. 7.10). The experimental set-up consists of a microwave source (transmitter), a probe detector and a metal reflector (a metallic plate for the reflection of microwaves), all placed in line. The waves coming out of the microwave source move towards the metal plate and are reflected back; the reflected wave and the incident wave superpose and create a stationary wave pattern. This can be detected by a probe detector placed between the transmitter and the metallic plate, and the intensity of the signal can be observed by the detector. You can move the plate or the detector to observe antinodes and nodes. By finding the distance from one antinode to the next antinode, the wavelength of the stationary wave can be found.
